In the era that followed, phase 1 of this evolution brought fresh perspectives on how software should be structured and maintained. The history of software engineering is a story of growing abstraction. Early programmers worked directly with machine code, flipping switches and reading blinking lights to understand what their programs were doing. As languages evolved from assembly to FORTRAN to C to Python, each generation of tools allowed developers to express ideas at a higher level without worrying about the underlying hardware. This progression did not happen overnight. Each step required not only new tools but new ways of thinking about problems. The discipline of computer science emerged from mathematics and electrical engineering, borrowing concepts from both while developing its own vocabulary. Algorithms, data structures, complexity theory, and formal verification all became part of a shared language that practitioners use to communicate across projects and organisations. Open source communities played a crucial role in spreading this knowledge, making production-grade tools freely available and encouraging a culture of transparency and peer review. Distributed version control systems revolutionised collaboration, allowing thousands of contributors to work simultaneously on the same codebase without overwriting each other's changes. Continuous integration pipelines automated the testing and deployment cycle, reducing the time between writing code and delivering it to users.
